title: Fasting safely
hookLine: the fast is not meant to harm, and health comes first

cards: A crowd on a road, gathered around one man. Someone is holding something over him to keep off the sun. The travelers are on a journey with the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, and the man in the shade is fasting.
Earlier we met the people the fast bends for, and the reason surah two gives: Allah wants ease for people, not hardship. What about someone who is fasting, and something starts to go wrong?

teach.h: A MAN SHADED ON THE ROAD.
teach.b: First, that scene on the road, in Sahih al-Bukhari. The Prophet sees the crowd and the man being shaded, and asks what's wrong. He's fasting, they say.
And the Prophet says it is not righteousness to fast while traveling. The man was keeping a fast he didn't have to keep, and it had brought him to where others had to shade him.

teach.h: A CUP OF WATER, RAISED UP.
teach.b: Second, a cup of water. A report in Sahih Muslim describes the Prophet on a journey in Ramadan, with people fasting and finding it hard. He calls for water, raises it so everyone can see, and drinks.
The fast he breaks is his own; the point is for the people watching: you may stop. Third, a principle.
A hadith in the collection of Ibn Majah says there is to be no harm and no harming. Jurists use that line as a rule of thumb: an act of worship that causes real harm has gone wrong somewhere.

So when someone fasting starts to feel faint, dangerously dehydrated, or unwell in a way that threatens their health, the books of law allow the fast to be broken and the day made up later. Fourth, the quiet part: asking.

teach.h: ASK A DOCTOR, ASK A SCHOLAR.
teach.b: People with diabetes, on medicine with strict timing, or recovering from illness may talk to a doctor before Ramadan, and to a scholar or imam. Some find a way to fast safely with changes.

Some are told not to fast at all, and feed the poor instead. Neither answer is a failure. The fast is worship, and the body that keeps it is a trust; in these hadith, taking care of it is part of keeping the fast.

how: Muslims with health conditions may consult a doctor and a scholar before Ramadan, and a person who becomes genuinely unwell while fasting breaks the fast and makes the day up later, or feeds the poor if they cannot fast at all.

o: fasting only in the cool months, when it's easier
drinking water during the day but not eating food
fasting without harm, and breaking it if harm comes

s: breaking a fast because you're genuinely ill is a failure of faith
the hadith show the Prophet telling people they may stop, and the day is made up later.
the Qur'an's verses about Ramadan say Allah wants ease, not hardship
"Allah desireth for you ease; He desireth not hardship for you" (2:185).
the Prophet drank water in public on a journey in Ramadan
a report in Sahih Muslim says he raised a cup so people could see, and drank.

games.q: you're traveling with the Prophet. a crowd has gathered to shade a fasting man. what does the Prophet say?
o: he should push through until sunset.
it is not righteousness to fast while traveling.
the others should fast harder for him.
games.why: it is not righteousness to fast while traveling. a fast that leaves you needing others to shade you isn't what the fast is for.

practice: Close your eyes if that's comfortable, and move your attention slowly down from the top of your head: is it clear or aching, is your throat dry, how do your stomach, back and legs feel?

Don't fix anything; just notice, the way you'd notice a friend's face across the table. If something has been asking for attention a while, a checkup put off, a medicine skipped, make a quiet note of it.

wordCard.voice: Fasting safely. Keeping the fast in a way that doesn't harm the body, and breaking it when it does, as the Prophet's own example shows. Today's word.

orig.note: 'no harm and no harming', the hadith in Ibn Majah.

carryVoice: Your line: not meant to harm. Ease, not hardship. Go gently today, and I'll see you tomorrow.

sources.q: Allah desireth for you ease; He desireth not hardship for you
